steps.title: The algorithm makes the list
steps.caption: Inside the victim PC, the malware computes 50 candidate domain names for today. It mixes the date with a secret key, hashes the result, and turns the hash into name-like strings. Nothing has touched the network yet, so DNS logs are still quiet. On the endpoint, a defender might only notice an unknown process that does a lot of hashing
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Silent queries begin
steps.caption: The malware asks the recursive resolver about the first candidate names, one after another. To the network this looks like ordinary DNS traffic from one host, except that every name is new and looks like keyboard noise. The resolver log now starts to collect the first pieces of evidence
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: NXDOMAIN answers
steps.caption: The resolver answers NXDOMAIN, which means "this name does not exist". The attacker registered only one name today, so most candidates are dead ends. A short burst of NXDOMAIN answers from a single host is the first strong signal a defender can see
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Candidate 13 is live
steps.caption: Candidate number 13 was registered by the attacker hours before the malware woke up. The resolver forwards that query to the attacker name server, which answers with an IP address. First-seen domain data now shows a brand-new name that nobody in the company has asked for before
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Beacon to C2
steps.caption: The malware reads the answer and connects to the C2 server behind the IP address. From now on it sends a small beacon about once per hour to say it is alive and to fetch orders. The DNS log shows the pattern clearly: many NXDOMAIN answers, then one success

steps.title: The seed rolls over
steps.caption: At midnight the seed changes, so the malware computes a completely new list of 50 names. Every blocklist entry from yesterday is now useless against today's traffic. The attacker only needs to register one fresh name each day to keep the channel open
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: The SOC sees the pattern
steps.caption: The SOC analyst reviews DNS telemetry and finds one host that asked 50 questions in six minutes and got NXDOMAIN for 49 of them - only one name answered. The names have high entropy, which means they look statistically random. The analyst opens a case and prepares containment
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Block the family, not one domain
steps.caption: The team blocks the family pattern instead of single domains, because new names appear daily. Using public research, they predict tomorrow's names and sinkhole them - they register or redirect the names first, so infected hosts connect to a controlled server instead. The victim host is isolated for cleanup
